Research model surfaced: Fusion GRU

Operational replay baseline: Persistence

Introduce the project as one auditable pipeline. Make the model distinction explicit: Fusion GRU is the research winner on the saved holdout, DCRNN is the graph benchmark, and Persistence remains the lightweight operational replay baseline.
Cross-border flow is a network problem, not a single-line problem. A local change can affect neighbouring countries and the routes available for recovery.
What is likely to happen in the next hour?
Use recent load and net-flow history, global network context, and graph centrality to forecast next-hour net flow.
What can we test when a link becomes stressed?
Reduce a selected transfer, search connected alternate paths, check headroom and loss, and report the trade-off for human review.

01  Build a canonical 12-node / 24-link graph from two supplied CSVs.
02  Compare transparent baselines, Fusion GRU, and DCRNN using chronological evaluation.
03  Add explainable graph-stress screening and recommendation-only rerouting.
Prediction estimates the next-hour condition. Prescription tests an action. The project never claims automatic switching or dispatch control.
Data, cleaning, features, and graph construction
Parse UTC → validate missing/duplicate/gap records → canonicalize aliases → align hourly histories → select 11 explainable features → chronological split → training-only scaling.
11 features = local flow, load, imbalance, residual + global flow/load/imbalance/residual + degree, closeness, betweenness centrality.

Fusion GRU
local + global + centrality → GRU → flow
24-hour lookback; hidden size 32; research winner by RMSE.
12 nodes jointly; 2 diffusion steps; hidden size 24.
No random shuffle crosses the time boundary. Model selection uses pooled RMSE; classification uses Normal / Warning / Critical labels.
Persistence is not persistent storage. It is a valid forecasting baseline. Fusion GRU and DCRNN are the advanced research experiments trained with the same leakage-safe target and holdout.
DCRNN preserves the country axis. At every hour, neighbouring information is diffused through the graph before a GRU-style update produces the next flow.

Fusion GRU is the research winner by RMSE, while Persistence has lower MAE and much lower inference time. This is why the interface distinguishes research model from operational baseline rather than hiding the baseline.
Training loss and macro-F1 are tracked across epochs. The validation curves show whether the model continues to generalize.
DCRNN uses the same target and chronological protocol but keeps the node axis and applies diffusion at each recurrent update.
Do not claim that a falling training curve alone proves production readiness. The important evidence is the shared chronological holdout and the comparison of validation/test metrics.
Rows = actual class; columns = predicted class. Off-diagonal cells show misses and false alarms.

Thresholds are not random: Warning and Critical are absolute net-flow magnitudes at the 75th and 90th training quantiles. Critical events are rarer, so F1, recall, ROC-AUC, and Precision–Recall complement accuracy.

text: Explain why accuracy alone is insufficient. A model can look accurate by predicting Normal frequently, while missing Warning or Critical cases. The saved confusion matrix exposes those errors.
The feature catalogue combines local time series, global network context, and static graph centrality.
Similar learned states should appear closer in the projected representation; overlap highlights difficult cases.
Interpretation principle: a model result is stronger when the audience can see which inputs, classes, and network structures shaped it.
Feature importance is evidence of sensitivity, not proof of causality. t-SNE is a visual diagnostic, not a performance metric.
Graph reasoning: stress propagation and resilience
Dynamic stress = 0.45 utilization + 0.25 endpoint risk + 0.20 propagated risk + 0.10 loss proxy. Criticality also includes betweenness and the topology impact of removing an edge.
These are transparent graph-screening artifacts. They explain influence and resilience, but they are not N-1 certification or AC power-flow validation.

Proxy only: replace assumptions with surveyed line geometry and engineering ratings before operational use.

1  Select a stressed edge
2  Move a chosen share of transfer
3  Remove the edge temporarily
4  Search connected alternate paths
5  Reject insufficient headroom / critical links
6  Score distance, utilization, loss, and risk
7  Report route, bottlenecks, and loss delta
Recommendation only: the planner does not switch equipment or dispatch generation.
Example: CH–DE → CH–AT–DE; 25% moved; best-effort review because proxy loss increases.
The prescription layer is a constrained what-if search. A route can relieve a stressed link while increasing estimated loss, so the UI exposes the trade-off rather than hiding it.

Next: connect verified telemetry, thermal ratings, AC power flow, and N-1 validation.

Final takeaway: Fusion GRU is the research winner; Persistence remains a transparent baseline; DCRNN tests the graph hypothesis; the system recommends evidence for human review, not automatic operation.

Close by stating the honest model hierarchy and the system limitation. Complexity is demonstrated through the trained Fusion GRU, DCRNN diffusion, evaluation evidence, and graph-prescriptive layer—not by hiding the baseline.
